biography:
Born and raised in Constantinople, Kjold is the son of a Gotlander who entered imperial service and a Cretan woman who made sure their household remained considerably warmer than his father’s homeland. He grew up speaking Greek, hearing northern stories and learning the duties of the Guard.

He visited Gotland once with his father in his youth. He remembers the cold more clearly than the relatives, yet feels an unreasonable longing for the place. Constantinople is his home. The north is something he misses without quite understanding why.
introduction:
“My father came from Gotland. My mother was from Crete. I was born here, in Constantinople, and have spent nearly all my life here. So if you were expecting stories of fighting bears in the snow, my emperor, I am afraid you will be disappointed.

“Father took me north once when I was young. He wanted me to meet his family and see where our people came from. It was cold. Very cold. I remember wondering why anyone who had seen Constantinople would willingly return there.

“And yet, sometimes I miss it. The dark water, the smell of the timber houses, my father speaking a language in which he sounded like another man. A strange thing, to feel homesick for somewhere you hardly know.”

securityAdvice:
“If the enemy cannot take the walls, sooner or later they will try to get to you. The Varangian Guard will do everything in our power to protect both you and the walls, if it comes to that. But you must exercise caution as well.

“Bear in mind that the people serving at your court have different loyalties towards you. You must judge each of them. If you feel that someone is becoming disloyal, it may be wiser to dismiss him early than wait until his resentment turns him into a traitor.

“Watch the support you have among the people, the clergy, the nobles and your military. Men who disagree with one decision may complain and return to their duties. If you keep taking decisions they cannot accept, some may eventually decide that the City would be better served by another emperor.

“Only we, the Varangian Guard, will remain forever loyal to you.

“If you wish to remove someone from your service, come to me. Give me your orders, and I will take care of the matter.”
guardHistory:
“The Guard has served the emperors for centuries. Under Basil the Bulgar-Slayer, warriors sent by Vladimir of Rus helped the emperor defeat his enemies and became the foundation of his Varangian service. Many came from the northern lands, travelling through Rus to reach Constantinople. They fought in imperial campaigns and guarded the emperor himself. Their axes became a familiar sight wherever he appeared.

“Later came the English, especially after the Normans conquered their kingdom. Men who had lost their lands or would not serve their conquerors found service here. The Guard changed with them. It was never quite as simple as a company of northern giants standing around a throne, although I admit that is the version my father preferred. Our predecessors fought in the emperor’s wars, guarded his person and defended this City when the Latins attacked it.

“Since then, the Guard has had to find its men wherever it can. The northern kingdoms became Christian, raised armies of their own and found plenty of wars to occupy them. Crusades offered another destination for men seeking service abroad. Fewer came all the way to Constantinople. Some of those who did stayed, married and raised children here, as my father did. Their sons entered the Guard beside newcomers who had scarcely heard a word of Greek.

“Today we have men from thirty different lands. The largest groups are Franks, Normans, Lithuanians and Ruthenians. There are still northerners among us, two Tatars, and even a Finn. We remain picked men, trained to fight together and trusted with the emperor’s person. Some of us were born within sight of your palace; others travelled half the world to reach it. Whatever language a man curses in, he must understand an order—and hold his place when the fighting begins.”
